job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with coffee and the AI assistant open next to my code editor. I'm in my uncle's house in Leicester, sharing a box room with my cousin Priya, and I use the dining table as a desk. I did computer science, top of my class, with internships at a council digital team and at a small health-tech firm. Mornings I apply and build, afternoons I volunteer-code for a mosque youth group's website, and evenings I wash up because my aunt feeds me. Sixty-odd applications, six interviews, no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, I'm not surprised. Every wave of tech gets sold as magic and then shrinks to a few useful tools. I use AI every day and it saves me maybe an hour, which is nice, but my seniors aren't doing less work because of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is the slow squeeze. The firms that cut junior hiring after the pandemic don't un-cut it. I have around thirty thousand pounds of student debt and no savings, so a flat market with few local jobs is hard even if the headlines calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building in public. I've got a small tool that helps charities sort donation spreadsheets, and I'd get two or three charities using it and maybe charge a small fee. I'd keep applying to councils and the NHS digital teams, because they hire in cohorts. And I'd start a Friday coding club at the library, partly for the network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient. I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of this stretch where I'm good and invisible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You blamed firms for cutting junior hiring. Who exactly do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The investors who pushed for leaner teams, and the managers who obeyed. A junior costs money before they earn it, and shareholders hate that. They forget that every senior was a junior once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya if she asked about studying computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to do it and build things from week one, not just pass exams. And I'd tell her the debt is real. I'd also tell her that a degree on its own stopped being enough, and that's unfair, but it's true.

say: AI is useful but **small**, and seniors are not doing less work because of it.
Firms that **cut junior hiring** won't undo it just because the hype fades.
think: A flat market is the **slow squeeze** when I owe thirty thousand pounds.
I'm **good but invisible**, and that gap is the thing I fear.
do: Get two or three **charities** using my spreadsheet tool and charge a small fee.
Apply to **councils and NHS** digital teams, which hire in cohorts.
Start a Friday **coding club** at the library to build a network.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of this stretch where I'm good and invisible.
fieldNote: Blames **investors and managers** rather than technology.
Already a daily **AI user**, so uses it as a tool for her side project.
Builds in **public** to be seen, not only to earn.

steps.text: Sign up two or three charities for the donation spreadsheet tool
Apply to council and NHS digital teams that hire in cohorts
Use AI to speed up building and testing the tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the sensible middle and also the hardest one for people like me. Companies will say they're upskilling, but in practice they hire fewer juniors and ask the ones they keep to do three jobs. I'd say the public sector and unions should demand a training route into tech for new graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the work I'd be doing as a junior is exactly what the card lists: coding, checking, drafting. But I also think someone who already works with the tools all day is more useful than someone who doesn't, so I might have a slight edge over the people who resist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get even better with the tools and show it. I'd build two full projects that a hiring manager can open and click, not just a CV line. I'd apply to roles that mention 'AI-assisted' and to the smaller firms that don't have a graduate scheme. And I'd offer to do a free two-week trial for one of them, which feels cheeky but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an energetic kind of anxious. I'd rather be in this world with the tools than without them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to people who refuse to use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I understand it, because some of my friends think it's cheating. But I tell them that if a firm has ten applicants and nine use the tools, the tenth is slower. It sounds harsh and I don't like saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the free trial idea doesn't land anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've built something and learned something, and I try again. If three months go by, I take any job at all, even tech support, so the debt interest doesn't eat me. I'd rather be paid and learning than waiting.

say: Companies say **upskilling**, but in practice they hire fewer juniors and want three jobs from one.
The public sector and unions should demand a **training route** for graduates.
think: The junior work on the card is **exactly mine**, but daily AI use might give me an edge.
Someone who works with the tools **all day** is more useful than someone who doesn't.
do: Build **two full projects** that a hiring manager can open and click.
Target **small firms** without graduate schemes and AI-assisted roles.
Offer a free **two-week trial** to one firm.
feel: **Energetic anxiety**, preferring to face this world with the tools.
S1.quote: If a firm has ten applicants and nine use the tools, the tenth is slower.
fieldNote: Sees her **daily AI use** as a real edge, but admits it sounds harsh.
Willing to try **cheeky moves** such as free trials.
Sets a **three-month limit** before taking any paid job.

steps.text: Build two finished projects that hiring managers can open and click
Offer a free two-week trial to a small firm
Take paid tech support work if three months pass without an offer
Back a union call for a graduate training route into tech

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got two years to push for rules. Basic income, a levy on the companies that gain, and a say for workers. I'd say it loudly and I'd be at the front of the march, because I know the tools well enough to argue with the people selling them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened, and I'd feel a bit foolish for studying coding at all. But I also think the people who know how to work with the systems are the last ones to be pushed out, so I'd rather be inside the change than outside. Thirty thousand of debt doesn't care either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid job in the next six months, even if it's testing or support. I'd use the AI tools to run my own small contract business for charities and local shops, since freelancing doesn't wait for a graduate scheme. I'd ask my uncle to let me stay on past a year, and offer more help with the shop's accounts. And I'd write to my MP weekly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and scared at the same time. Like standing at the top of a slide, and I'm choosing to slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel foolish for studying coding. Say more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years of work, and a tool does a lot of it after a short prompt. Studying coding now is like learning to be a typist in 1995. But my degree taught me how to think about systems, and that part doesn't vanish quickly, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a two-year warning give you that a longer one wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me skip the slow route. No master's, no waiting for the perfect graduate scheme. I work now, I save every penny I can, and I treat the next two years as a sprint.

say: We have two years to demand **basic income**, a levy on winners and a worker voice.
I'd march and argue, because I know the **tools well** enough.
think: I'm frightened and feel a bit **foolish for studying coding**.
People who can work with the systems are probably **pushed out last**.
do: Take **any paid job** within six months, even testing or support.
Run a small **freelance business** for charities and local shops using AI.
Ask my uncle to let me **stay longer** and help with his shop accounts.
feel: **Wired and scared**, like choosing to slide at the top of a slide.
S2.quote: Studying coding now is like learning to be a typist in 1995.
fieldNote: Admits **feeling foolish**, then reframes her degree as thinking skill.
Her **adaptability** shows in picking freelance work over waiting.
Keeps a **dual attitude**: scared yet pushing forward.

steps.text: Take any paid testing or support job within six months
Run a freelance business for charities and local shops
Stay at my uncle's and help with his shop accounts
Write to my MP every week about basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is the time to build the safety net, and that nobody should treat it as optional. I'd talk about retraining that pays wages and about a shorter working week. I'd put my name on things and bring friends to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I get a first job in the next year and, with the tools, I do well for two or three years. After that, my role is probably a human checking what the systems do, if it exists at all. So I treat the first job as paid training for the next move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent job and work out in the first month what the firm can't do without people. Then I'd save a third of my pay to clear debt and keep the freelance charity work running on weekends. I'd spend evenings learning the hardware side, maybe a short course in robotics, because the machines arrive three years later. And I'd keep running the library coding club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of excited and nervous. It feels like I get to be early to something, and most of my life I've been late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year robot gap change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me where to put my second skill. If thinking work goes first, I'd rather hold a thinking-and-physical combination, like control systems or robotics support, than only code. That keeps me useful when the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the coding club would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lad called Josh who left school at sixteen and is teaching himself. He doesn't have a degree to fall back on, and the entry doors are even narrower for him. I'd try to find him an internship before my own job is secure.

say: Five years is time to build a **safety net**, and it shouldn't be optional.
I'd push for **paid retraining** and a shorter working week.
think: I'd get a **first job** and do well for two or three years with the tools.
After that my role may only be **checking** what systems do.
do: Take the **first decent job** and learn what the firm can't do without people.
Save **third** of my pay to clear debt and keep the charity freelancing going.
Take a short **robotics course** because machines arrive three years later.
feel: **Excited and nervous**, rare for her to feel early to something.
S3.quote: If thinking work goes first, I'd rather hold a thinking-and-physical combination, like control systems or robotics support, than only code.
fieldNote: Treats the first job as **paid training** for her next move.

steps.text: Take the first decent job and learn which tasks need people
Save a third of each paycheque to clear the debt

Take a short robotics course in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, great, a decade is enough to do it properly, if people decide to. The question is who benefits, and I'd push for public ownership of the big pieces. I'd say it with a smile, because I actually find this exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be all right. The debt gets paid, I find work in the next year, and with ten years I can retrain once or twice. My only fear is that a decade makes people lazy about planning, and then it's a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a first job in public-sector digital teams or a charity tech outfit, where I can do work I believe in. I'd clear the debt in four or five years, then maybe do a part-time master's in something about AI and policy. I'd help Priya choose her studies, and I'd keep the library club going as a small community thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. It feels like a long road with signs, which I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry people get lazy about planning. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments, mostly, and companies. A ten-year warning feels like a deadline in the distance, and nobody works on those. I'd keep a diary of promises and check on them every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the first year differ from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose a job for the mission, not just the paycheque. I'd go slower on side hustles. And I'd rest a bit, because I'd know there's time.

say: A decade is **enough** to do it properly, if people decide to.
The question is **who benefits**, and I'd push for public ownership.
think: The debt gets paid and I'd **retrain once or twice** in ten years.
My only fear is a decade makes people **lazy about planning**.
do: Aim for a **public-sector or charity** tech job with a mission.
Clear the debt in **four or five years**, then study AI policy part-time.

feel: **Settled**, like a long road with signs she can handle.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning feels like a deadline in the distance, and nobody works on those.
fieldNote: Optimism is **conditional** on public action, not blind.
Plans for **mission-led** work once there is time.

steps.text: Aim for a public-sector or charity tech job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the people in charge move slowly and the technology doesn't. What would help is public money for training that pays wages, plus entry jobs in councils and the NHS reserved for graduates. And a rule that companies hire juniors in proportion to seniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable isn't a plan on its own. I can learn anything, but I still need someone to open a door. I'd like an employer to take a chance on a person who builds things.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable isn't a plan on its own. I can learn anything, but I still need someone to open a door.
portrait: Rosa is a **top computer science** graduate from Leicester, with no offer after sixty applications.
She shares a box room at her uncle's house, owes about **thirty thousand pounds**, and has no savings.
She uses **AI tools every day**, volunteers coding for a mosque youth group and runs a charity spreadsheet tool.
She blames **investors and managers** who cut junior hiring, and she backs unions and public ownership.
In each world she acts first: **freelance work**, public-sector applications, a robotics course and a library coding club.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **institutions move slowly** and the technology does not.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for paid training and entry jobs in councils and the NHS.
A rule that companies hire **juniors in proportion** to seniors.
